brief: Six habits that quietly cost a team its week

slots.eyebrow: On where the week actually goes
slots.subline: Six habits that look like diligence, cost about a day each, and survive because everyone assumes somebody chose them.
slots.heroTitle: Every one of them was a reasonable decision that nobody revisited.
slots.heroBody: About a day a week, each

slots.slideTitle: It was booked for a problem that got solved
slots.slideSubtitle: Recurring meetings outlive their reason by default, because cancelling one requires somebody to decide it is no longer needed and nobody is rewarded for that decision.
slots.leftValue: Five people, one hour, every week
slots.rightValue: Cancel it once and see who notices

slots.slideTitle: Writing it takes longer than reading it
slots.slideSubtitle: A weekly summary is written carefully by one person and skimmed by six. The information was already in the tool; the update exists to prove work happened, not to transmit anything.
slots.leftValue: An afternoon of the clearest thinking
slots.rightValue: Link the board and write three lines

slots.slideTitle: Added after one incident, kept forever
slots.slideSubtitle: Every sign-off was introduced the week something went wrong. It prevents that specific failure and taxes every unrelated piece of work for years afterwards without anyone auditing it.
slots.leftValue: Two days of waiting on one message
slots.rightValue: Name what it prevents, or drop it

slots.slideTitle: Polishing before anyone has seen it
slots.slideSubtitle: The work feels safer the longer it stays private, which is exactly backwards: the expensive mistakes are the ones a five-minute conversation would have caught in week one.
slots.leftValue: A fortnight, spent in the wrong direction
slots.rightValue: Show it while it is still embarrassing

slots.slideTitle: A quick question is never quick
slots.slideSubtitle: The asking takes a minute and the answering takes twenty, because the person answering has to rebuild the context they just lost. Being available is not the same as being useful.
slots.rightValue: Batch them. Answer twice a day

slots.slideTitle: Removing all six would not make you fast
slots.slideSubtitle: These are symptoms of a team that cannot tell which work matters. Cut them from a team that still cannot tell, and you get the same confusion with more hours to spend on it.
slots.leftValue: Nothing, if the priorities are clear
slots.rightValue: Fix what you are building first

slots.subline: Pick the recurring one you would not defend if somebody asked you to justify it, and skip it once without announcing anything.
slots.heroTitle: If nobody notices, you have your answer. If somebody does, you have a better meeting.
slots.signoff: The other five follow the same test — the only real question is whether anything breaks when it stops.
